intuition: Try to spell the word by walking through neighboring board cells. Each move must match the next letter, and a cell cannot be reused within the same path. Mark a cell while exploring from it, then restore it when that path ends so another path can use it.

The recursive state consists of a coordinate and the next word index. A mismatch or out-of-bounds coordinate immediately rejects that branch. On a match, temporarily mark the square unavailable and search the four neighbors for the next character. This marker represents only the current path’s occupancy.

Restoration is as important as marking. A failed path must not prevent a different starting cell or a different branch from using the same board cell. Restore before returning even when a complete word was found, so the caller receives its original board.
The terminal index condition means all earlier characters have already matched; it does not require stepping onto an additional square.

Before searching, reject a word longer than the board or needing more copies of any letter than are available. These are necessary conditions, not proof of adjacency: passing them still requires the full path search.

An optional refinement can search the reversed word when its final letter is rarer than its first; reversing a legal path preserves adjacency and no-reuse, reducing the number of candidate starts. The reference retains forward traversal for a consistent walkthrough.

steps: For word="ABCCED", start at the A in board row 0, column 0.
Match B at (0,1), then C at (0,2), marking each visited square so this path cannot return to it.
The next C is directly below at (1,2). From there, E at (2,2) extends the matched prefix.
D at (2,1) completes the six letters. The next recursive index equals the word length, establishing success.
Unwind the recursion and restore every marked letter. Return true for the valid A→B→C→C→E→D path.

codeNotes.note: The temporary marker blocks only cells already on the current recursive path, preventing illegal reuse without a separate visited set.
A neighboring coordinate is searched against the next character, preserving adjacency and character order together.
Restoration runs after both successful and failed searches, so sibling paths and future calls see the original board.

keyDecision: The next cell must share a side, match the next letter, and be unused in this path.

concept.question: Can a word be spelled along one path without revisiting a square?
intuition: Letter counts alone cannot establish a word: its letters must be adjacent in order. A promising partial route may also become impossible, so cells must be released when exploring another route.

Start from a matching first letter. Walk through side-adjacent matching letters, temporarily reserving each visited square. If a continuation fails, release its squares and try another neighbor. A reservation belongs only to its current path.
concept.observation: A cell can be used once within a path; moves must share a side and match the next letter.
approach: Reserve a matching square and explore side neighbors for the next letter.
Restore on return; succeed after all letters are matched.
concept.correctness: Each explored path matches a prefix of the requested word and uses distinct adjacent cells. Trying every legal matching neighbor includes the next move of any valid full path. Releasing cells after a branch restores the board for other starts and routes. Completing every letter therefore proves existence; exhausting the starts proves absence.

complexity.explanation: Try each starting cell, then potentially several neighbors for each next letter. Worst-case work is exponential in word length times board area. The current reserved path needs memory proportional to its length.

pitfalls: A cell can be used once within a path; moves must share a side and match the next letter.
Matching counts cannot override the one-use rule.

scenes.narration: Continue down to C at (1,2), then E at (2,2).
scenes.decision: A previously used square is reserved for this path and cannot be reused.

scenes.narration: Move left to D at (2,1). The full path A→B→C→C→E→D spells the word, so answer yes.
scenes.decision: Restore reserved cells while unwinding, even after a successful search.
